on behalf of the gue/ngl group, wildlife crime, such as poaching and illegal trade in species or illegal transit of wildlife products and derivatives, is now taking on an international dimension, placing it among the largest and most profitable illegal activities in the world. according to the resolution under discussion, the turnover associated with these crimes amounts, on an underestimate, to at least 19 billion dollars a year. as long as demand remains high and enforcement efforts are reduced, legitimate trade will continue to serve as a front for illegal trade and to stimulate poaching. in addition to a direct threat to the survival of several species, these crimes entail significant dangers to native ecosystems, for example from the uncontrolled spread of exotic species into the environment. the european union, which is both an important market and a transit route for illegal wildlife trade, has responsibilities in combating this phenomenon, which it must not undermine. in addition to strengthening efforts to enforce and strengthen international conventions, it is necessary, in a framework of enhanced cooperation between member states, to adapt the legal frameworks, in particular as regards sanctions, to pursue policies that discourage the consumption of products from vulnerable wild species and to support the recovery and conservation of wild species populations, and to combat poaching involving local communities, in particular in developing countries.
mr president, in recent years there have been cases of fraud in the food chain in the face of the failure of existing control systems. from horse meat, which has become beef, to dioxin contamination, to the entry into the food chain of products derived from cloned animals in an unauthorized manner, to the adulteration of alcoholic beverages, to products advertised as organic which are not, among other examples. these are scandals which show the increasing weakening of basic principles of public health, consumer rights, food quality and safety. this weakening is not only due to the inadequacies of the existing regulatory and control framework, but is above all inseparable from the growing deregulation and liberalization of agricultural and trade policies, the resulting complexity and increased extension of food chains, and the models of intensive export-oriented production that favour large-scale agribusiness and annihilate small and medium-sized farming. it is not enough to talk about regulation and control. scandals will continue - some known, others hidden - as long as these policies and production models are not radically changed.
mr president, it is clear to us that the rights of the selfemployed must be safeguarded and guaranteed. but this should not hide one of the biggest problems, one of the biggest realities, which is the fact that a large proportion of these selfemployed people are not really and in fact selfemployed. in several countries, like my own, in portugal, a significant proportion of these workers are fake self-employed because they have a supervisor, they have a fixed work schedule, they have a fixed salary, but they don't have a contract with rights. the vast majority of these workers have a permanent job but no actual contract. and these workers are mainly young people who see their lives mortgaged, they are workers who pay their social security and all the taxes, because the companies, many of which are often state-owned, do not want to take on their responsibilities. we largely agree with this report, but we cannot accept that those who should be working effectively should not see their rights guaranteed.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the budget is properly managed. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this programme must put the consumer at the centre of the single market, in the full exercise of his rights. consumers must be well informed about their rights and how to exercise them and have full confidence in the various players in the single market. this is a way, a good way, to boost economic growth in the european union. in this connection, i proposed that the commission should establish a set of statistical indicators at eu level to assess and improve the functioning of the single market. this programme must contribute to the protection of the health, safety and economic interests of consumers, and promote their right to information, education and organisation in defence of their interests.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i should like to begin by congratulating mr rochefort on the excellent work he has done on this important report. when european consumers are empowered to make informed choices, the single market is strengthened and innovation and growth are stimulated. that is why consumer policy is a key pillar for achieving the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. european consumers need to reap the full benefits of the single market, to have full confidence in its functioning, to feel that their safety is guaranteed and that there are legal mechanisms to defend and protect them. in this regard, this programme, which will run for the next six years, will strengthen accessibility to alternative dispute resolution mechanisms through exchanges between bodies and by improving the dissemination of best practices. financial support for consumer organisations is being continued, and the provision of information to consumers is being improved and improved, in particular by providing reliable and easily accessible internet sites, including price comparison. a platform for consumer education exchange is established. with this new approach we are ensuring that consumers have a high level of protection, that their rights are respected, that they are placed at the centre of the european single market. in conclusion, this programme makes the citizens of the union much more cautious because they are the reason for the existence and functioning of the single market.

in writing. - i welcome this report, given that i believe that in the current economic, financial and social crisis and with scarce budgetary resources, the capacity for innovation is essential. i believe that innovation plays a key role in job creation and growth. i would stress and reiterate that investment in research is one of the thematic objectives of cohesion policy. in this context, i believe that the regions should set priorities for the financing of research and development. in my view, the regions should invest in research and innovation by promoting and enhancing their own strengths and comparative advantages. i believe that in order to achieve the objective of smart specialisations, greater synergy between universities, businesses and regional and local authorities should be encouraged.
in writing. − in a context of severe recession in europe, solutions are urgently needed to increase european competitiveness in a globalised world. these solutions cannot be achieved by re-applying the development models used in the past, but rather by a european commitment to specialisation and innovation, for the creation of added value. within the eu too, and as i have been arguing, states can only be competitive and aspire to meaningful economic growth if they specialise in what they do best. it makes no sense to have 28 states competing with each other in producing the same product or providing the same service, when these same 28 states are different and have different economic models and natural and social conditions. on the contrary, each of them should choose the one that best suits his own model and his own circumstances. with 28 competitive and growing states, the eu will also be more competitive on a global scale.
in writing. − smart specialisation is the way in which a region can take advantage of comparative advantages by taking into account its strengths and setting r&d&i priorities. the vision expressed in the report, which is in some ways the same as that which guided the adoption of the regulations on the structural funds for the period 2014-2020, deserves several points of criticism. the regions are being pushed to develop the so-called smart specialisation strategy, or else they will no longer receive the funds earmarked for operational programmes. if the priorities are not well defined, taking into account market developments, the region will have difficulty in developing this concept and consequently its financing may be called into question. if the priorities are right, taking account of market developments, then it is not the regions that set the priorities but those who guide the market's progress - the monopolies that rule the european economy. however much the report may spin around some of the concepts, in the end there will be regions which risk being excluded from the bulk of cohesion funding if they do not take up these same concepts. once again, the conditionality... we do not deny that there are positive aspects to this report. but the differences we have on some key aspects are obvious.
in writing. − in this era of economic recession and consequent budgetary shortages, as well as increasingly tough global competition, it is crucial for the eu to sustainably improve its capacity for innovation. in future, the use of the different european structural and investment funds should be facilitated by a common framework regulation. in addition, the common use of the european structural and investment funds should be particularly facilitated under horizon 2020, in particular to facilitate the participation in that programme of regions that still show considerable deficiencies in terms of research infrastructures and thus to close the innovation gap between the most advanced and the least favoured regions. that is why i am voting in favour.
in writing. − in the new 2014-2020 programming period, both member states and regions should invest in research, development and innovation (r&d&i) through smart specialisation. i voted in favour of this report because it allows for a more efficient future use of structural funds, such as the erdf, which are essential for the economic and social development of the regions for the next programming period.
in writing. − the european union needs to improve its capacity for innovation in a sustainable and effective way. to this end, this paper introduces the concept of smart specialisation, whereby a region, taking into account its strengths or comparative advantages, sets priorities for research, development and innovation. the strategy should ideally focus on activities that span several sectors and technology domains with effects on the regional economy. there should also be active cooperation between all the actors, from research to the administrative level in companies. the rapporteur also advocates interaction between regions, which could be beneficial in enhancing the union's competitiveness. for these reasons, and because i believe that the strategy promotes an effective cohesion policy, i voted in favour of adopting this document.

in writing. - this report deals with the way in which the european parliament exercises its powers under the treaty of lisbon in practice. the areas where parliament's consent is required are: association agreements, accession agreements, agreements establishing a specific institutional framework, agreements with significant budgetary consequences for the eu, adoption of the multiannual financial framework, application of the flexibility clause, establishment of enhanced cooperation, uniform procedure for the election of members of the european parliament, composition of the parliament and implementing measures for the eu's own resources system. in all these cases, although parliament's consent is required, under conditions which may vary (simple or qualified majority), in none of these areas can parliament change the content of the proposals submitted to it only approve or reject them. in practice, certain procedural questions have arisen which are now being clarified by revising the rules applicable to the rules of procedure with a view to establishing the approval procedures. the rapporteur proposes, for legal clarity, that the approval/rejection procedure be formally separated from the reasoning and recitals accompanying the decision, which are now to be set out in a separate resolution/recommendation drawn up by the relevant committee. we are not opposed to the solution found.
in writing. - the approval procedure constitutes, with the treaty of lisbon, a special legislative procedure within the meaning of article 289 (2) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, which is exhaustively codified. the voting practices and the content of reports in the context of the approval procedures have changed and it was necessary for the rules of procedure of the european parliament to incorporate these updates.
in writing. - this report deals with the way in which parliament gives its consent in cases where the consent of the european parliament is required under the treaties (consent procedure). the cases in which the approval procedure applies are exhaustively defined by the treaties. the aim of this report is to standardise the approval procedures by revising the applicable rules of the rules of procedure with a view to clarifying the approval procedures, making them more transparent and possibly more effective. i therefore support this initiative and have voted in favour of this report.

in writing. − the main objective of this report is to bring the abovementioned council regulation into line with articles 290 and 291 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu). the final result of the negotiations with the council, which we are voting on today, has not substantially altered the initial report. it only, regrettably, reduces the time of parliament to object to a delegated act. the report is in essence an adaptation of the treaty of lisbon, but it must be examined in the light of the profound significance of the treaty, particularly in the field of commercial policy. the lisbon treaty stipulates that trade policy is an exclusive competence of the eu. in other words, the states have been deprived of an essential instrument of economic policy. the interests in the commercial field are, of course, different from country to country, because the respective economies, fragility and potential of each country are different. the overlapping of the interests of the strongest with those of the weakest, in this as in other areas, entails tremendous damage to weaker economies, as is the case with portugal. the effects of free trade policies on the restructuring of important national productive sectors are illustrated.

in writing. - the main objective of this report is to bring legislation in this area into line with the changes introduced by the lisbon treaty. the final outcome of the negotiations with the council does not introduce any substantive changes. however, the time available to parliament to object to a delegated act has been reduced. however, this report must be assessed in its deeper meaning, taking account of the positions of principle on the treaty and its provisions on trade policy. the lisbon treaty stipulates that trade policy is an exclusive competence of the eu. the interests in the commercial field are, of course, different from country to country, because the respective economies, the fragility and potential of each are different. the overlapping of the interests of the strongest with those of the weakest, in this and other areas, is detrimental to weaker economies, as in the case of portugal, which is in the hands of the commercial interests of the economic groups of the eu powers, especially germany, which are often opposed to the interests of the national productive fabric. in this particular case, we are dealing with an example of import of a product crucial to portugal, and the criteria for safeguarding the interests of each country in determining the import conditions are obviously different depending on the country.

in writing. - this report is based on the commission proposal on the harmonisation of three council regulations on imports of olive oil and other agricultural products from turkey with the post-lisbon treaty regime on implementing and delegated acts. a whole series of legislation in the field of the common commercial policy is in the process of being harmonized through two regulations, the procedures for which are still in progress and will be the subject of negotiations between the two co-legislators. in the interests of legal consistency, parliament proposes amendments concerning the participation of the european parliament in the preparation of delegated acts, the limitation of the delegation of power to the commission for a period of five years, with tacit extension for an equal period, and the extension of the possible extension of the period for objecting to a draft delegated act from two to four months, thus extending the examination period from four months (2+2) to six months (2+4). i have no objection to voting in favour of this procedure.
in writing. - the commission proposal aims to align council regulations (ec) no 2008/97, (ec) no 779/98 and (ec) no 1506/98 on imports of olive oil and other agricultural products from turkey, as regards the delegated and implementing powers to be conferred on the commission by articles 290 and 291 tfeu which set out the new regime of delegated and implementing acts. among the various amendments tabled, the call for parliament to be involved in the preparation and implementation of delegated acts is noteworthy. for the reasons i have given, i voted in favour of the document.

in writing. - i approve this report in view of the fact that aromatised wines are of great economic importance in the wine sector of the european union, with traditional producers well established in many member states. these are important issues relating to the rules for the definition, description, presentation and labelling of aromatised wine products and the establishment of criteria for the recognition of geographical indications. i would remind you that the european union accounts for 90% of the global production of aromatised wine products. i agree that this proposal should update the legal framework for this economic activity and give substance to the geographical indication of aromatised wine products. i also believe that there is a clear need to update the existing rules in the light of technological developments, innovation, market developments and consumer expectations in relation to quality and production methods.
in writing. - i am completely in favour of the restriction on the standards for the sangria name. i am particularly pleased that this concerns only beverages produced in portugal and spain. protecting the term sangria is to maintain a reference to an instantly identifiable drink anywhere in the world. any other country wishing to produce this drink will have to add to the name sangria the complement of the sales denomination of the aromatized wine-based drink, in addition to the name of the member state where the drink was designed.
in writing. the report by mr bartolozzi deals with the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the definition, designation, presentation, labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products. it updates the sales denominations and brings them into line with consumer information legislation. the text also aligns european standards with the requirements of the world trade organisation (wto). aromatised wine products play an important role for consumers, producers and the agricultural sector in the european union in general. the eu accounts for about 90% of the world's production of aromatised wine products (about 3 million hectolitres per year). in this report rules were approved which only allow the sales denomination sangria to be used in drinks produced in portugal and spain. the purpose of this measure is to protect the term sangria, which originates from the two iberian countries, by limiting its use by other member states to supplementary and optional product information. this sales denomination may therefore only be used in portugal and spain. i think that the updates to the regulation on the definition, designation, presentation, labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products were equally important.
in writing. − the main objectives of the proposal are to improve the applicability, readability and clarity of eu legislation on aromatised wine products through specific criteria for product designation, contributing to a well-defined quality policy. the report provides safeguards for protected geographical indications, not allowing any kind of misleading information, nor labelling with words such as style, type, etc., when a product does not meet the established prerequisites. it protects sales denominations, such as the sangria denomination, which can only be used if it is produced in portugal or spain (otherwise the label must state that it is a wine-based flavoured product). it protects consumers by allowing only the use of wine ethyl alcohol, and the data relating to its sugar content (dry, extra-dry, sweet, etc.) may be added to the sales denominations, but always in accordance with the standards and percentages established. as regards quality policies, it is provided that member states may lay down more stringent rules on production and description. for all these reasons, and especially in order to provide greater protection and information to consumers, to prevent misleading practices, to comply with the standards of transparency, we voted in favour.
in writing. - aromatised wine products play an important role for consumers, producers and the agricultural sector in the european union in general. they represent a significant part of the european wine sector and constitute a very important market from a qualitative and quantitative point of view, both domestically and internationally. this proposal for a commission regulation aims to update regulation (eec) no 1601/91 laying down general rules on the definition, description and presentation of aromatized wines, aromatized wine-based drinks and aromatized wine-product cocktails.
in writing. - aromatised wine products play an important role for consumers, producers and the agricultural sector in the european union in general. they also represent a significant part of the european wine sector and constitute a very important market from a qualitative and quantitative point of view, both domestically and internationally. the eu accounts for around 90% of the world's production of aromatised wine products (around 3 million hectolitres per year), with traditional productions rooted in many member states, mainly in the central and south, but also in the north and east of the continent. by this regulation, the european parliament adopted rules restricting the sales denomination sangria to beverages produced in portugal and spain. the protection of the term sangria, which originates in these two countries, is included in the updated regulation on the definition, designation, presentation, labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products. in agreeing with this measure i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. - in the present case, and at the time of the vote, i followed the indication of a vote against expressed by my political group. the justification is that there is a loophole in this legislation which allows sangria, as a product of portuguese or spanish wine, to be made with grapes or wine from outside these countries, the origin of these grapes or wine being further disguised by the additives traditionally used in the confection of this product. this does not ensure proper consumer information or the necessary support for local wine production, which should be the objectives of the legislation. this vote does not, however, mean that i am against the protection of the sangria designation of origin as being specifically portuguese or spanish. i am in favour of protecting the origin of this product, as is the case with other traditional products of certain geographical origins. for the reasons set out above, i believe that legislation could and should have gone further in protecting the interests of consumers and producers.
in writing. - aromatised wine products play an important role for the agricultural sector in the european union. the proposal aims to update the general rules on the definition, designation and presentation of aromatised wines, aromatised wine-based drinks and aromatised wine-product cocktails marketed in the european union. the rapporteur calls for greater clarity in legislation on these products and the introduction of a well-defined quality policy. another objective is also alignment with the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu) by applying uniform rules on geographical indications, administrative and physical checks and the exchange of information. i voted in favour of this document.

in writing. - i approve this report, taking into account the amendments made to the original proposal. i believe that carbon capture and storage technology should not be seen as competitive in the european energy network, although i recognise its importance in terms of co2 reductions from industrial sources such as steel, iron, chemicals, cement and refineries. i believe that carbon capture and storage technology should remain a decision of the member states. i support the idea that energy efficiency and renewable energy should remain the main focus of european legislation, for the benefit of the environment and the mitigation of climate change. i also believe that carbon capture and storage technology should be considered as a transitional solution in reducing greenhouse gas emissions from industrial sources.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on carbon capture and storage, as i believe that this technology could provide a transitional solution to ensure emission reductions in certain industries. i believe, however, that european climate policies and their funding programmes should continue to focus on renewable energy and energy efficiency.
in writing. − the deployment of carbon capture and storage (ccs) has the potential to enable the eu to meet its 2050 targets for reducing carbon emissions at the lowest cost, and is a necessary tool, especially to reduce co2 emissions from highly polluting industries. ccs could also contribute to the diversity and security of energy supply, while maintaining and creating employment opportunities. i also believe that we must find ways of ensuring that technology is used to play a role in combating the threat of global warming.
in writing. − the report by colleague chris davies is on the 2013 implementation report: development and application of carbon capture and storage technology in europe. co2 separation and capture technology has been around since the 1930s. the transport of co2 by pipeline is common worldwide. in sleipner, norway has been injecting 1 million tonnes of co2 into the deep, rocky north sea soil every year since 1996, with no sign of any unexpected movements. i believe that if we want to promote innovation, reduce costs and accept this technology as a viable option then we have to come to an agreement in a way that focuses thinking and encourages the use of some of the existing funds. we should therefore support the development of a range of flagship projects in the field of carbon capture and storage. i believe that this technology has an important role to play in combating the threat of global warming.
in writing. − all paragraphs in this report support the idea that carbon capture and storage (ccs) is a key tool, an appropriate, reliable and useful technique, which needs to be supported by urgent public and private investment in climate policy. we have serious doubts about the urgency of promoting a method and a technique which still needs to be studied and developed further and which, at its present stage of development, has very significant impacts on the environment, in addition to very high costs. the report recognises the technique as economically advantageous mainly for the big polluters, industries that emit large amounts of carbon dioxide (co2). we support investment in research and in the study of methods and techniques useful for reducing the atmospheric concentration of co2, as will be the case with cac. but it will not be just a method or technique that will solve the problems of increasing atmospheric co2, as this report might lead you to believe. we do not consider cfc to be the key response to achieving the objective of keeping global temperature rise below safe limits, as the rapporteur does. we voted against it.

in writing. - the expectations of the european union to become the world leader in the deployment of carbon capture and storage (ccs) were very high five years ago. not only had the european council embraced the idea of having up to 12 ccs demonstration projects in operation by 2015, but it had also approved a proposal by the european parliament for a financing mechanism (ner300) that appeared to be able to provide sufficient public support to ensure the realisation of these projects. however, there were few concrete results. in this report, parliament proposes ways of ensuring the application of a technology which has a role to play in combating the threat of global warming. i have voted in favour of this report, in accordance with the objectives.

in writing. - in recent years, several scandals in the food chain have come to light, ranging from the substitution of key ingredients for cheaper ones, to the mislabelling of animal species, to the presence of chemical contaminants, in the face of the failure of the entire existing regulatory and control framework. these are scandals which show the increasing weakening of basic principles of public health, consumer rights, food quality and safety. this report proposes the definition and scope of food fraud, identifies the factors contributing to its occurrence and possible solutions to strengthen eu surveillance systems. it proposes the development of an eu reference laboratory for food authenticity, among other measures. without questioning the goodness and relevance of some of the proposed measures, it is not enough to talk about regulation and control to safeguard the basic principles mentioned above. changes in production models and policies are needed. these situations are inseparable from the increasing deregulation and liberalization of agricultural and trade policies, the increasing complexity and extension of food chains, and the export-oriented, intensive production models that are destroying small and mediumsized farming and local production and consumption. all this is ignored in the report.

in writing. − labour inspections are of fundamental importance to protect workers' rights, ensure health and safety standards at work, prevent breaches of employment protection standards and ensure fair competition in the european union. the establishment of an electronic network between all the social services involved is supported, which will facilitate the exchange of data between the competent authorities when carrying out inspections. the committee also calls for the development of national action plans, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, to strengthen labour inspection mechanisms and improve the continuing training of inspectors. for the reasons i have just given, i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − the fight against illegal work and poor health and safety conditions at work must be a priority for all responsible administrations, and inspections to ascertain the legality of the situation of workers and the compliance of their working conditions with legal requirements are an inalienable obligation and an important factor in regulating and assessing business activity and the degree of respect for workers' rights. however, they cannot and should not be used as a tool against the economy or to curb economic initiative and activity by imposing on firms excessive or unreasonable rules or obligations which discourage recruitment and investment. biblically, separating the wheat from the weeds does not mean merely burning the latter, but is intended, above all, to let the former grow and become stronger. it is therefore necessary to abandon the dickensian and eighteenth-century idea of what firms are and to support and encourage their work, while still subjecting them to inspections wherever this proves justified and appropriate.
in writing. - this report focuses on the need for labour inspections and their increased frequency, to protect workers' rights and improve working conditions. we agree with the rapporteur that, in view of the increase in atypical and precarious employment contracts, the increase in undeclared work and crossborder work, it is necessary to ensure that sufficient resources are available to strengthen labour inspections. however, we must not forget that austerity measures are contributing to the deepening of the economic and social crisis in countries with weaker economies, by imposing a degradation of labour relations, accompanied by disregard for labour laws and workers' rights. this is largely ignored in the report. today, workers are forced to work in any conditions and the health and safety conditions at work have suffered from the civilizational regression to the level of rights at work. prevention, proper supervision, public investment, combating the precariousness of employment which is always associated with the occurrence of accidents and the absence of health and hygiene conditions at work, and the criminalisation of accidents at work are urgent steps. difficult to achieve with eu policies which increasingly devalue and degrade workers.
in writing. - the economic and social transformations of the last few decades have had a dramatic impact on the world of work. the globalisation of the world economy has had negative effects on traditionally safe and fair labour relations. subcontracting, outsourcing, precariousness, intensification and job insecurity have been undermining the quality of employment in europe. this gradual degradation of industrial relations has been accompanied by a disregard for labour laws and workers' rights. the eu has been confronted with the reality of undeclared work and the shadow economy. the inspection mechanisms need to safeguard the interests of workers, especially in this period of crisis that the eu is going through.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the steinruck report on labour inspection because i think it is important that workers' rights and labour standards (in particular safety and health) are effectively guaranteed throughout the union. the legal asymmetry between the various member states in this respect is sufficient. it is important that it is not aggravated by the lack of means of enforcing the domestic legislation of each member state. the situation of undeclared work and of false selfemployed persons is a particularly worrying case of evasion of the employers' labour obligations. the economic integration of the union must be accompanied by an equivalent level of social integration, otherwise regulatory competition will put pressure on countries with higher levels of labour protection to reduce them so as not to lose economic competitiveness vis-à-vis countries with lower labour standards. the greatest danger to the european social model, in its aspect of labour rights, is the toleration of social dumping, whether legal (due to a lack of rights) or de facto (due to a lack of means of effectively enforcing social rights). the enforcement of labour rights is therefore an official matter of the union's labour constitution.
in writing. - the economic and social transformations of the last few decades have had a dramatic impact on the world of work. the globalisation of the world economy has had negative effects on traditionally safe and fair labour relations. subcontracting, outsourcing, precariousness, intensification and job insecurity have been undermining the quality of employment in europe. this report, which i voted for, proposes that eu-level legislation be taken to regulate new forms of work and atypical work, to define clearly and bindingly the status of workers in the eu, in order to combat the most common practice of breaching labour law, namely false selfemployment. this measure will be an important tool for labour inspectors to determine whether companies are resorting to this illegal practice.
in writing. − over the last decade, the european union has been confronted with the gradual degradation of labour relations through realities such as undeclared work and the shadow economy. both have negative consequences for the economy, which are manifested in the poor quality of products and services, the lack of productivity of enterprises and the promotion of unfair competition in the single market through the loss of tax revenues. the report also calls for the eu to take action to combat the spread of the virus and to ensure that the virus is contained in the body. the report also calls for the establishment of a european agency responsible for cross-border matters in the field of labour inspection. the creation of a european social security card and an early-change system, which allows the exchange of information between authorities in the event of fraud or illegal exploitation, is also mentioned. i voted in favour of this report because i am a strong supporter of decent and fair working conditions.
in writing. - this report focuses on the importance and need for labour inspections and their increase, both to protect workers' rights and to improve working conditions. we agree with the rapporteur that, given the increase in atypical and precarious forms of employment contracts, the increase in undeclared work and crossborder work, it is necessary to ensure that sufficient resources are available to strengthen labour inspections. however, we must not forget that it is the austerity measures that are contributing to the deepening of the economic and social crisis in countries with weaker economies, imposing a degradation of labour relations which has been accompanied by disregard for labour laws and workers' rights. today, workers are forced to work in any conditions and the health and safety conditions at work have suffered from the civilizational regression to the level of rights at work. prevention, proper supervision, public investment, combating job insecurity, which is associated with the occurrence of accidents and the absence of health and hygiene conditions at work, and the criminalisation of accidents at work are urgent steps. difficult to achieve with eu policies which increasingly devalue and degrade workers. we voted yes.
in writing. - i approve this report, considering that it is necessary to plan and provide for a set of minimum operating requirements for the system of financial participation by employees in the profits of companies. it is necessary to ensure that employees who participate financially in the company's profits are properly informed about the underlying risks, both in terms of rights and duties. i believe that the system of financial participation by employees in the company's profits should ensure equal conditions of integration.
in writing. − employee financial participation allows employees to share in the success of the enterprise in which they have invested, thus contributing to improving their satisfaction and performance. indeed, greater employee responsibility for the management of the company contributes to its stability and growth. because of the risks and responsibilities associated with participation in this type of scheme, it is essential that clear information is provided to employers and workers to enable them to decide and evaluate the best options. i voted in favour of this report on workers' financial participation in the capital and profits of enterprises, taking into account their positive contribution to the fight against unemployment and economic growth.
in writing. − in view of the serious economic crisis the eu is going through, and in particular the difficulties that several european companies have been facing, i believe it is necessary to look at alternative forms of participation in companies. i therefore agree that financial participation by employees is an option to be considered by the member states, which can provide greater participation by employees in decision-making and strengthen good governance.
in writing. the report covers three main models of employee financial participation in enterprises (efp): profit participation (cash, deferred or equity); individual employee participation in capital (employee shares and stock options); and employee participation plans (esops). in any of these schemes, workers who opt for pft acquire the right to enjoy the benefits of the company's success, but also share in the responsibility and risks, particularly those 'linked to strategic decisions'. the report calls on member states to remove transnational obstacles to increasing the financial participation of employees in companies. it advocates a gradual convergence of existing ftt regimes and related national legislation. it advocates that employee participation schemes be made available to smes to meet their particular needs. in short, we are faced with a concept and proposals which are extremely controversial. the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the pft is a firm in difficulty. the concepts explained here are, moreover, inseparable from a line of conditioning of wages and workers' rights, including the rights and role of their representative organizations, such as trade unions.
in writing. − financial participation by employees in the profits of companies can be a good mechanism to increase their incomes and, on the other hand, to increase workers' productivity levels. legislation is therefore needed at european level to remove transnational barriers to the implementation of ftts, such as double taxation. that's why i'm in favour.
in writing. − the eu 2020 strategy for smart, inclusive and sustainable growth stresses the need for inclusive growth that, among other things, empowers citizens through employment, investing in professional skills, fighting poverty and modernising labour markets and social protection. this report addresses worker financial participation, an instrument that provides a tangible means of developing these issues through greater participation of workers in decision-making in the companies for which they work, helping to strengthen good governance and ensuring that they receive a share of the financial benefits of a successful business activity. this instrument can also strengthen smes by providing innovative financing mechanisms, as workers may wish to invest in shares of the company they work for, capitalizing on the expansion. i voted in favour of this report because i agree with this mechanism.
in writing. − employee financial participation (efp) is a way of helping to strengthen good governance in companies, as they participate in the decision-making process in the companies. this participation also develops the long-term view, as workers become more involved in the decision-making process and employers therefore feel more incentivised to invest in vocational training opportunities for their workforce. the rapporteur stresses that this participation can also strengthen smes, as workers have the possibility to invest in shares of the share capital of the company for which they work, making jobs safer. participation in ftts is currently relatively low and the fact that these benefits vary across sectors, company size, worker demographics and member states needs to be reinforced. the document also proposes that the european union develop a framework concept of general guidance on basic principles and best practice to help facilitate the acceptance of ftps in the member states.
in writing. - the so-called financial participation of employees has the fundamental objective of creating a false illusion among the employees that they have the power to make decisions on the company's strategies. in fact, the financial participation of workers in enterprises means, in many experiments, the conditioning of workers' wages and rights, including trade union rights. and it takes away the responsibility of those who have always profited from running the company - the bosses. we voted against it.
in writing. - i approve this report, as i believe that the current crisis is putting increased pressure on social protection systems in many member states. i believe that, given the current economic difficulties associated with the economic crisis in the european union, it is necessary to ensure that minimum standards of social protection are met for all eu citizens. in this regard, it is necessary to strengthen social protection, in particular for self-employed workers who in many member states are excluded from social protection schemes, placing them in an unequal situation in social terms and on the labour market. i believe that the social protection of selfemployed workers should be guaranteed in such a way as to allow, for example, access to unemployment funds, medical assistance, among other rights to which they are denied, in a clear devaluation of the status of selfemployed. by protecting the social rights of the selfemployed, entrepreneurship and self-employment are being promoted, which is desirable in a dynamic and potential eu market.
in writing. − the increase in expenditure linked to demographic change is threatening the social security systems of the member states. these systems are still facing increased social costs linked to high unemployment rates in several member states. in the face of these challenges, it is urgent to continue the modernisation of social security systems in the european union in order to ensure access to high quality health systems and the most efficient use of public resources. the reality of women in the labour market must be taken into account. women, more often than men, interrupt their careers to care for children, the elderly, dependents or sick family members. this may lead them to opt for parttime or lower-paid jobs, with a negative impact on their pensions. self-employment must be recognised and adequate social protection measures must be introduced. it is important to ensure that self-employment does not become a means of preventing workers from benefiting from social security, nor a way for employers to circumvent labour and social security legislation. for these reasons i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in recent years, several member states have had to initiate programmes or implement measures to ensure the long-term sustainability of their social security system or equivalent. however, there seems to be a disparity in the social protection afforded to workers in employment and to self-employed workers in certain member states. although social protection policy is the responsibility of each member state, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, there seems to be the necessary space for a responsible discussion to take place.
in writing. - the report by mrs vilija blinkevičiūtė focuses on social protection for all, including the self-employed. social protection is important and its main function is to promote social inclusion and social justice, protect wages and ensure quality education and healthcare services for all. social protection policy is the responsibility of each member state, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. however, at eu level, the open method of coordination has been adopted, which, in a voluntary process of political cooperation, allows common objectives and indicators to be defined. these objectives have their natural origin in the fundamental values of the european union. among other measures proposed in this report, i believe it is important to combine efforts to combat the fake selfemployed and to encourage the social partners to exchange good practice on services for the selfemployed.
in writing. - it is clear to us that selfemployed workers must have their rights assured and guaranteed - something which is not the case today. but there is an inescapable fact that must be emphasized here. in reality, many of these workers are not truly selfemployed. today, in several countries, notably in portugal, there is a significant proportion of false selfemployed, who follow a hierarchy, who have a fixed work schedule, who have a fixed salary, but who do not have an employment contract with the rights that are inherent in it. the vast majority of these workers have a permanent job but no effective link. we largely agree with this report. we are in favour of extending social protection to selfemployed workers and sanctions against employers who hire workers under the guise of selfemployment. however, we do not follow the references to the need to reform social security systems (we know what that means...), to raising the retirement age and to flexicurity.
in writing. - social protection is at the heart of the european social model. its main function is to promote social inclusion and social justice, protect wages and ensure quality education and health care services for all. social protection policy is the responsibility of each member state, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. however, at eu level, an open method of coordination has been adopted, a voluntary process of political cooperation based on the adoption of common objectives and indicators. one of the main objectives of social protection is to increase the equity and effectiveness of services, while promoting social inclusion and cohesion as key elements of inclusive and sustainable growth and poverty reduction. these objectives have their natural origin in the fundamental values of the european union. it is the maintenance of these principles that we must preserve, regardless of whether we go through a period of crisis which may lead to their being forgotten. that is why i am voting in favour.
in writing. − in 2012, self-employment accounted for more than 15% of total employment in the eu. this report, which i voted for, stipulates that the increase in selfemployment must be accompanied by adequate social protection measures for these workers. social protection is at the heart of the european social model. its main function is to promote social inclusion and social justice, protect wages and ensure quality education and health care services for all. this report also indicates the need to continuously optimise and modernise social protection systems at member state level in order to ensure sound, sustainable and adequate social protection for all, including the selfemployed.
in writing. − social protection and social security for all are at the heart of the european social model. the absence of a clear definition of selfemployment and of recognition at european level is detrimental to them in terms of social security. in europe, traditional social security systems were designed to ensure the protection of employees, which is why this regularization aims to ensure better protection for the middle class: the economically dependent self-employed worker. however, it should be borne in mind that this is a very heterogeneous group, since it includes both self-supporting persons or professionals in certain sectors who receive a considerable remuneration, as well as persons whose activity depends on a single client, among others. the rapporteur stresses that the lack of a link between national and european legal frameworks in the distinction between paid employment and the provision of services makes the concept of self-employment a problematic issue. everyone has the right to social protection, and that is why i voted in favour of this document.
in writing. - it is clear that selfemployed workers must have their rights assured and guaranteed. but this should not hide one of the biggest problems of these workers - that in reality these workers are not self-employed. today, in several countries, notably in portugal, there is a significant proportion of false independents, who follow a hierarchy, who have a fixed work schedule, who have a fixed salary, but who do not have a contract with rights. the vast majority of these workers have a permanent job but no effective link. we largely agree with this report. we are in favour of extending social protection to selfemployed workers and sanctions against employers who hire workers under the guise of selfemployment. however, we do not follow the references to the need to reform social security systems, to raising the retirement age and to flexicurity. that way, we abstain.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate my fellow rapporteurs and all those who have collaborated with them on the excellent work which has resulted in an important legislative reform in the union. the need for a modern and up-to-date regulatory framework in the field of concession award and public procurement was therefore all too evident. in fact, these contractual instruments are important levers for the completion of the single market, thus contributing to the promotion of economic growth and job creation. the aim is to ensure that economic operators take full advantage of the freedoms introduced by the single market when participating in public procurement or in the award of concessions within the european union. these objectives are achieved by, first, simplifying the rules and adapting them to the ever-changing political, social and economic contexts; second, by facilitating the access of small and medium-sized enterprises to the public procurement market, which allows contracting authorities to widen their supplier base and these small and medium-sized enterprises to increase their turnover and thus promote the creation of new jobs; and third, by reducing the legal uncertainty surrounding the award of these concession contracts. these new provisions will enable authorities to make better use of these instruments in support of environmental, energy efficiency and climate change policies. the new legislation also makes a decisive contribution to transparency and, as a result, to combating favouritism, corruption and conflicts of interest.
madam president, commissioner barnier, the combination of the two directives on concession contracts (the juvin report) and on public procurement (the tarabella report) is a balanced instrument for advancing and modernising the single market, removes the previous legal uncertainty associated with in-house service, allows for the efficient use of public resources, preserves the advantages of high-quality services provided by public entities, imposes social, labour and environmental requirements on providers, dematerializes bureaucracy, and ensures that subcontracting is bound to the same obligations as the main contractor, preventing harmful or even fraudulent disclaimers. in general, the new directives promote healthy competition in public procurement and concessions. the selection criteria are based on the principle of choosing the most economically advantageous offer rather than the one with the lowest cost, which allows social, environmental and quality of service attributes to be introduced into the price-quality ratio. it is therefore excellent legislation.
madam president, i also want to begin by thanking the rapporteur for his work, because i believe that the amendments tabled by the european parliament improve the commission's text and respond to the main concerns of the social partners. more transparency and clear rules avoid distortions in the internal market. for example, direct contract adjustment promotes fraud, national favoritism and corruption. concession contracts should therefore be public and transparent. the implementation of the directive must respect the promotion of quality employment, ensure adequate social protection and combat social dumping in the award of cross-border concessions. it is necessary to ensure that the main international social and environmental conventions are integrated into and respected in the concession award procedure.
madam president, for a long time now, there has been a convergence of very voracious appetites on public procurement, on the huge market for public contracts, appetites which are inseparable from the advance of the market in areas where the states traditionally exercise their social function through public services, and the arguments are repeated even though reality insists on refuting them. the need for clarity and transparency in public procurement is not at issue, but public procurement. it is good to remember that they are an important instrument for defending employment with rights, promoting and stimulating economic activity and preserving the environment, that is, everything that is threatened by the subjection to the rules of free competition in the single market which the european commission's proposals always sacralize and hence also proposals always tailored to large companies and not to small and mediumsized enterprises.
first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on this balanced compromise which is being proposed to the house. access to external public markets is essential for european companies, especially in the current economic crisis. however, the public procurement market in the union is very open to foreign companies, but access by european companies to international public procurement markets is far from similar. the way to solve this asymmetry is not to close our market, as the radical left proposes, but to try to open external markets. the aim of this initiative is not to close the european market to foreign firms but to open external markets to european firms. it is not a measure restricting international trade but an incentive to open up international trade. the union's interest in protecting the objective of economic growth and job creation by european companies must not be sacrificed by any national interest in benefiting from cheaper offers from countries which do not offer the same opportunities to our companies, whether in china, brazil, india or russia. a very important point i would like to make in the caspari report, and which is common to the tarabella and juvan reports discussed this afternoon on public procurement legislation, is the mandatory compliance with labour rights and social and environmental standards both at national and union level, i.e. external economic operators must comply with the applicable environmental, social and labour obligations in the performance of public contracts, which will contribute to establishing fairer conditions in the union's public procurement market. in conclusion, the aim of this initiative is to ensure openness and reciprocity in international trade and it has our support for this.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group, the amendment to the honey directive now proposed was motivated by a court of justice decision in relation to a complaint from beekeepers whose honey was found to contain pollen from genetically modified plants. although pollen is not an ingredient in honey but a naturally occurring addition to it, there is a clarification that is intended to be introduced into the legislation, there is a decision that has to be taken at the outset. what can be done about the cause of this, namely the presence of gm pollen in honey? and here are two options: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he considers this a real problem and whether he thinks that it should be solved in the best possible way, or whether he considers it normal that honey can be marketed containing gm pollen in any quantity, without any measures being taken to prevent it and without the consumers even being aware of it. we are not ignoring the problem. the proposals we have made seek to solve this problem in the best possible way, without forgetting, however, that the problem can hardly be solved entirely in a framework such as we have today, in which the release and large-scale cultivation of genetically modified organisms in the wild is allowed. this being one of the many profound implications of the release of gmos into the wild, it cannot, of course, be resolved except in a wider framework of questioning the gmos themselves and their effects on health and the environment.
madam president, commissioner, i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur on his excellent work. the industry is faced today with a number of constraints and difficulties, such as the problem of lack of funding and excessive regulation. first, it is essential to create the conditions for increased investment. the crucial instrument in this area is the eu budget, which places a high-impact political priority on reindustrialisation, i.e. science, innovation, education and support for smes. secondly, the competitiveness of european industry needs to be improved through smarter regulation, less red tape and structural reforms in growth-friendly member states. thirdly, a new innovation policy is needed to encourage faster development and commercialisation of goods and services. that is why horizon 2020 covers the entire innovation cycle, from fundamental research to the first steps of market entry. and one of its three pillars is entirely devoted to industrial competitiveness. finally, i would like to mention the importance of the internal market. we must deepen and complete the internal market, and in particular in three key areas: energy, services and the digital agenda. only a global response will unlock the potential of european industry and make it a driver of growth and job creation.

in writing. - i approve this report, convinced of the need for a european legislative initiative on concessions. the lack of legal certainty, the persistence of direct contracts awarded without regard to the broad principles underlying the internal market of the european union and the legal patchwork at member state level in this area make it necessary to establish a legislative framework at european level. however, this framework should take a light approach to setting clear, coherent, understandable and effective rules. public procurement represents a very important part of economic activity in the union. public procurement and concessions are the most frequent forms of public procurement. public procurement is subject to clear rules. on the contrary, concessions are simply governed by the general principles of the treaty and by a wealth of case law. in my view, a legislative initiative in the field of concessions offers the advantage of clarifying the existing legislative framework in the face of the multiplication of the case law of the court of justice of the european union and strengthens legal stability and security in the face of the legal mosaic that exists in the eu due to the lack of uniform application of the principles of the treaty.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the juvin report on the public works and services concession directive because it fills an important gap in the union's legal order. the fragmentation of national regimes in an area which is central to competition in the internal market on a level playing field could not be maintained. the directive obviously safeguards in-house concessions and public-public partnerships where there is no real outsourcing of public management. it is clear that the directive does not oblige any public authority to grant any public works or public service, which is a sovereign matter. the award of a concession is always optional, but if the competent authority decides to award a public works or service, it must comply with common rules throughout the union. i therefore see no reason for excluding public water concession contracts, and no reason for keeping them exempt from the new union regime. an important feature of the new scheme is the obligation to respect labour rights and environmental obligations in force in the union and the member state concerned, which is especially relevant for competitors from outside the union (but not only).

in writing. - i consider honey to be a natural, healthy product. a potential labeling as containing genetically modified pollen in the ingredients would damage the reputation of honey. by defining pollen as an ingredient, consumers may think that pollen is a distinct product that is added to honey, when this is not the case. moreover, classifying pollen as an ingredient would considerably increase the costs of the tests carried out to obtain the information necessary for labelling, harming amateur beekeepers even more than professional beekeepers, considering their small-scale production. i would point out that the cjeu's conclusion remains valid. genetically modified pollen honey, as defined in article 3 (1) (c) of that regulation, is a food produced from gmos. this means that the amount of genetically modified pollen allowed for the application of the 0,9% labelling threshold will have to be calculated as a percentage of the total amount of the single ingredient honey, and not as a percentage of the total amount of pollen. the 0,9% limit applies to food and organic producers. in this sense, there will be an inequality of treatment between beekeepers and organic producers, which would not be fair.
in writing. - this report concerns the proposal to amend the honey directive, based on a ruling by the court of justice, in relation to a complaint by beekeepers whose honey was found to contain pollen from genetically modified plants. the court's decision to consider pollen as an ingredient in honey has implications for small producers which should not be ignored, such as the increased cost of testing to obtain the information needed for labelling. although pollen is not an ingredient of honey but a naturally occurring component of it (a clarification which is intended to be introduced in the legislation), consumer information on the presence of gm pollen in honey should be ensured through labelling. and measures should be taken to avoid as far as possible the occurrence of gm pollen in honey. that is the spirit of the amendments we have tabled, which unfortunately have been rejected by the majority. even though we know that the problem can hardly be solved entirely in a framework such as we have today, in which the release and large-scale cultivation of gmos in nature is allowed, it was possible to go further and not simply ignore the problem of gm pollen in honey.
in writing. - i do not agree with the provisions of this directive, as i believe that the consumer should be aware, on the labelling of products, of their composition and whether or not they contain genetically modified components. in the case of honey, if the pollen is known to originate from genetically modified plants, this should be mentioned on the label and made known to the consumer.
in writing. - i voted against this report because i felt that the protection of european beekeepers producing honey without the presence of pollen from genetically modified plants and flowers, and the potential value of their production, were not guaranteed. the text adopted does not allow for a distinction to be made between honey produced from pollen from gmos and honey produced from pollen free of gmos, nor does it allow for consumers to be adequately informed about the true composition of the honey they buy and consume. although it is generally against the classification of pollen as an ingredient, i believe that such a designation should be given when it comes from gm plants and flowers and has a presence of more than 0.9%. a final reason why i am against the text adopted in plenary is that this directive makes it possible to mix honey produced in europe with honey from other geographical areas, without any reference to its origin and composition, and does not adequately protect european beekeepers.

in writing. − the hercule iii programme is a multiannual action programme to promote action against fraud, corruption and other illegal activities affecting the financial interests of the union for the period 2014-2020. this programme will fund competent entities such as national and regional administrations, research and education institutes and non-profit organisations, both in the provision of technical assistance and in training to meet the general objective of protecting rigor and transparency in the use of public funds. the legal basis for hercule ii expired at the end of 2013 and its replacement is intended to ensure the continuity of european support for activities carried out by the commission and the member states to provide better information, to carry out studies and to provide training and technical and scientific assistance in the fight against fraud. we voted in favour.

november 2002. we are therefore dealing with agreements concluded more than a decade ago. when these two agreements were signed, they were among the most advanced and ambitious trade agreements in the european union. since then, however, the trade policy context has changed significantly on both sides. the union has embarked on a dynamic negotiating agenda for bilateral trade agreements, including in the americas, in particular with central america, colombia and peru. it has recently concluded negotiations with canada, is negotiating the transatlantic trade and investment partnership with the united states and is still actively negotiating with mercosur. mexico and chile, for their part, are engaged in the negotiations on the trans-pacific partnership, are members of the pacific alliance, on the european union side, the latest generation of trade agreements, starting with korea, are much more ambitious in terms of their scope and the depth of trade liberalization. it is enough to environmental standards, which is now a mandatory part of the union's trade agreements. we have this joint debate today on the trade agreements with mexico and chile, and exactly to what extent do madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the recognition of ecological damage by european and international legislation is an indispensable first step towards taking a position that is becoming increasingly necessary in the face of the real and serious risk of ecological disasters. many have been those resulting from marine pollution caused by oil spills, whether by accident, shipwreck or sinking of ships, among which is that of the prestige. the environmental devastation is then enormous, with a strong impact on marine and coastal biodiversity, as well as great economic and social damage to coastal communities. today, a growth in maritime transport of more than 3% per year, with ever larger ships, contributes to a significant increase in the risk of accidents at sea. another factor that increases the risk is the increasing number of extreme weather events in the context of climate change. the protection of coastal regions and their populations requires that the possibility of ecological disasters caused by marine pollution be taken into account, and that effective mechanisms be established to compensate for the damage caused by the serious and long-term impact on the environment and marine resources of traditional activities such as fishing, aquaculture, sea fishing, nautical tourism and bathing, as well as emerging maritime activities in the blue economy. in this context, in addition to the necessary compliance with the established polluter-pays principle, it is essential to adapt european and international legislation to include a concrete definition of the concept of ecological damage and its liability, with a view to allowing an effective and rapid mitigation of the negative impacts of ecological disasters, as well as the creation of a specific european fund for compensation for ecological damage resulting from marine pollution caused by the massive oil spill in shipping accidents.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, honourable members, thank you very much for your comments. on behalf of the commission, i can assure you that these comments are taken into account by the commission. you also underlined the construction of ships and substandard ships, and after the prestige and erika accidents, much work has been done to improve the quality and resistance of ships, so we should not ignore this either. regarding the polluter pays principle and the existing legislation, the existing international conventions on liability for oil pollution play a very important role in upholding compensation claims for environmental damage. when it comes to recognition and reparation of environmental damage, the eu and its member states have traditionally led efforts to raise international standards, and we have been successful in raising these standards in the past. this is why we now have a very comprehensive international regime at our disposal in the event of maritime accidents. in the pursuit of constant improvement, the eu is looking into the available information on accidents at sea which have resulted in environmental damage. the environmental liability directive establishes a comprehensive definition of damage to the environment or ecological damage, including that which occurs in water. under eu law, there is no distinction to be drawn between ‘environmental’ and ‘ecological’ damage. during 2014, the commission is due to report to parliament and the council on the outcome of its study on the effectiveness of the environmental liability directive.

in writing. - the negative points outnumber the positive guidelines for the reindustrialisation of europe presented in this extensive document. the example of this is the panacea for all ills - the deepening of the single market and liberalization: energy, telecommunications, transport, eco-products, venture capital, etc. all this is properly integrated into the european semester process and the national reform programmes, thus legitimised, as are the structural reforms (of labour and production markets in order to reduce labour costs, the weight of wages in national income and state intervention in the economy) they advocate. the use of public-private partnerships and the formation of smart specialisation clusters, including transnational and regional clusters, in an increasingly open and liberalised market environment are also advocated. what portugal needs is an industrial policy which gives priority to the development of national production, taking into account the country's specific development needs and valuing and enabling the development of smes. this will not be possible without a determined, committed and vigorous intervention by the state, without a state policy to support the industrial development of the country. we voted against it. in view of the liberal orientation of the report, it remains to add that the rapporteur is from the green group.

in writing. - the negative aspects of the report are much more serious than the positive ideas for the reindustrialisation of europe which this extensive document presents. the european union's well-known panacea for all ills is an example of this - the hallowed liberalisation of the single market for the most diverse sectors: for goods, energy, telecommunications, transport, green products and venture capital, alongside alignment with the failed europe 2020 strategy and integrated into the european semester process and the national reform programmes. the use of public-private partnerships and the formation of smart specialisation clusters, including transnational and regional clusters, in an increasingly open and deregulated market environment are also given priority, i.e. the same ingredients that led portugal and other countries to the economic ditch, which has resulted in a highly burdensome policy for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (smes). we are in favour of an industrial policy which gives priority to the development of national production, of the strategic sectors defined by each country, the dynamisation of its industry, taking account of the specific development needs and valuing and enabling the development of smes.
